headline: Millions in Spain stop work over high rents

sources.title: Millions join Spain's first general strike in 14 years in protest at housing crisis (The Guardian)
Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike (BBC News)
Spain's general strike demands solutions to housing crisis (NPR)
Millions of Spaniards stage first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing (CNN)

chunks.text: On November 11, 2026, millions of people in Spain stopped work for 24 hours. It was a [[general strike]], a protest in which workers across the country stop work the same day. It was Spain's first general strike in 14 years and the first mainly about housing. Unions said it {{shut down}} many car factories and [[ports]]. In Spain's second-biggest city, protesters {{put up}} [[roadblocks]] on highways.

verbs.correct: To make a place stop working
verbs.wrong: To clean a place after work
verbs.why: The city shuts down the pool every winter. A big storm often shuts down the airport. Unions said the strike shut down many car factories and ports in Spain on November 11, 2026.

verbs.wrong: To hide something under the ground
verbs.why: Workers put up a fence around the new park. The city puts up lights on every main street in December. In Barcelona, protesters put up roadblocks on highways during the strike.

chunks.text: [[Tenants' groups]], organizations for people who rent their homes, first planned the strike. Spain's two largest [[labor unions]], groups that speak for workers, later {{got behind}} it. [[Public anger]] over rents grew in late September, after an 87-year-old woman was [[evicted]], or forced to leave, from her apartment in Spain's capital. She had lived there for 70 years. Her rent had [[tripled]] after new [[landlords]] {{took over}}. She died weeks later. Protests {{sprang up}} across Spain.

verbs.correct: To support a plan or a group
verbs.why: Most parents get behind the plan for a new school. Fans get behind their team when it plays at home. Spain's two largest labor unions got behind the strike that tenants' groups first called.
When a new boss takes over, the rules often change. A big company sometimes takes over a small family store. The woman's rent in Madrid tripled after new landlords took over.
New coffee shops spring up all over town. Small tents spring up in the park before the summer fair. After the woman was evicted, housing protests sprang up across Spain.

chunks.text: Rents in Spain have {{gone up}} about 80% in ten years. In the capital, a small apartment of 50 [[square meters]] cost 1,170 euros a month [[on average]] in October, a [[property website]] reported. The average [[gross salary]] in Spain, or pay before taxes, is about 2,460 euros a month. So in the capital, rent can {{eat up}} nearly half of an average worker's pay. [[Housing experts]] say rent should take no more than 30% of pay. A 36-year-old hospital worker in the capital said he still cannot {{move out}} on his own.

verbs.why: Bus fares go up almost every year. The price of coffee goes up when the weather is bad. Rents in Spain have gone up about 80% in ten years.

verbs.correct: To use a large part of something
verbs.why: Car repairs eat up most of my savings. Long meetings eat up half of her workday. In Madrid, rent for a small apartment can eat up nearly half of a worker's pay.

verbs.correct: To leave home and live somewhere else
verbs.wrong: To swim across a wide river
verbs.why: Many young people move out when they start college. My sister moves out next month because her new job is in another city. A 36-year-old hospital worker in Madrid said he still cannot move out on his own.

chunks.text: Tenants' groups said about 4 million people joined the strike by midday. About 120,000 people {{turned out}} to march in the capital in [[heavy rain]], officials said. Storms made unions {{call off}} marches in some southern cities. Business groups and the capital's [[regional government]] {{spoke out}} against the strike. Tenants' groups want the government to {{crack down on}} [[housing speculation]], buying homes only to sell or rent them for more money.

verbs.wrong: To watch an event on TV
verbs.why: Thousands of fans turn out for the big parade every year. Few people turn out for the town meeting when it rains. About 120,000 people turned out to march in Madrid in heavy rain, officials said.

verbs.wrong: To pay for a planned event
verbs.why: Schools often call off classes when it snows. The team calls off practice when there is lightning. Storms made unions call off marches in some southern cities in Spain.
Many doctors speak out against smoking. Some students speak out when a school rule seems unfair. Business groups and Madrid's regional government spoke out against the strike.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To pay people to do something
verbs.why: The police crack down on fast drivers near schools. Some cities crack down on loud parties at night. Tenants' groups want the government to crack down on housing speculation in Spain.

wordDefs.def: The government of one part of a country, not the whole country
ex: The regional government pays for local hospitals.

mainIdea.s: Millions of people in Spain stopped work for a day to protest high rents. In Madrid, a small apartment can cost nearly half of an average salary, and renters want the government to act.
mainIdea.why: The general strike was mainly about housing. Rents have gone up about 80% in ten years, and rent can eat up nearly half of a worker's pay.

mainIdea.s: Spain's first general strike in 14 years was mostly about the cost of homes. Business groups strongly supported it and marched beside the unions to ask for cheaper places to live.
mainIdea.why: Close, but business groups did not support the strike. They spoke out against it, while tenants' groups and the two largest unions got behind it.

mainIdea.s: Spain's government opened thousands of new low-cost apartments for young renters in Madrid. Officials say families can move in next spring and the rents will stay low for many years.
mainIdea.why: This is about a one-day general strike over high rents. Millions of people stopped work, and the strike shut down many factories and ports.

tf.s: Millions of people in Spain stopped work to protest high housing costs.
tf.why: It was a general strike mainly about housing, and unions said it shut down many car factories and ports.

tf.s: Spain's two largest labor unions spoke out against the strike.
tf.why: The unions got behind the strike. Business groups and Madrid's regional government were the ones who spoke out against it.

tf.s: Housing protests sprang up after an older woman was evicted from her home.
tf.why: Public anger grew after an 87-year-old woman was forced to leave her Madrid apartment, and protests sprang up across Spain.

tf.s: Rent in Madrid can eat up nearly half of a worker's pay.
tf.why: A small apartment costs about 1,170 euros a month, while the average pay before taxes is about 2,460 euros.

tf.s: Rents in Spain have stayed about the same for ten years.
tf.why: Rents have risen about 80% in ten years, and rent can now eat up nearly half of a worker's pay in Madrid.

tf.s: Spain's business groups got behind the general strike.
tf.why: Business groups did not support it. They spoke out against the strike, while tenants' groups and unions backed it.

lines.text: Did you hear about the big strike in Spain?
I did. Millions of people stopped work for a whole day, right?
Right. And it was mostly about housing. Rents there are [[through the roof]].
In Madrid, rent for a small apartment can {{eat up}} almost half of someone's pay.
Half? [[I don't blame them]] for being angry.
Rents have {{gone up}} about 80% in ten years.
Wow. So what started all this?
An 87-year-old woman lost her apartment in Madrid. Her rent tripled after new landlords {{took over}}.
That's awful. I guess people finally said [[enough is enough]].
Exactly. Protests {{sprang up}} everywhere, and the two biggest unions {{got behind}} the strike.
Did a lot of people {{turn out}}?
About 120,000 marched in Madrid, even in heavy rain. Storms made unions {{call off}} some marches in the south.
Marching in a storm? That takes a lot of energy.
Not everyone was happy, though. Business groups {{spoke out}} against the strike.
So what do the renters want?
They want the government to {{crack down on}} people who buy homes just to make money. And one hospital worker said he still can't {{move out}} on his own at 36.
[[Sounds familiar]]. My cousin is 30 and still lives with his mom.

expressions.def: Very high, much higher than normal
ex: Gas prices are through the roof this summer.
After the new park opened, home prices went through the roof.

expressions.def: Used to say that you understand why people feel or act a certain way
ex: They want a bigger apartment. I don't blame them, with three kids.

expressions.def: Used to say that a bad situation has lasted too long and must stop
ex: After the third late train this week, I said enough is enough and bought a bike.
The neighbors decided enough is enough and asked the city for help.

expressions.def: Used to say that you know a similar situation from your own life
ex: Your landlord raised the rent again? Sounds familiar.
He works two jobs and still can't save money. Sounds familiar.
